| How do I add a new column to an existing table?                                    | ["Altering a Table\nYou can use ALTER TABLE  to modify an existing table.\nAdd a Column\nDrop a Column\nModify a Column Type\nMove a Column to the First Position\nTo move a column (e.g., email) to the first position:\nTo move a column after another column (e.g., move gender after name):ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE ;\nALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN is_active ;\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (150);\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR (100) FIRST;\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other') AFTER name ;", 'Working with Tables in MySQL\nSelecting Data from a Table\nSelect All Columns\nThis fetches every column and every row from the users table.\nSelect Specific Columns\nThis only fetches the name and email columns from all rows.\nRenaming a Table\nTo rename an existing table:\nTo rename it back:SELECT * FROM users ;\nSELECT name , email FROM users ;\nRENAME TABLE users TO customers ;\nRENAME TABLE customers TO users ;', "Inserting Data into MySQL Tables\nTo add data into a table, we use the INSERT INTO  statement.\nInsert Without Specifying Column Names (Full Row\nInsert)\nThis method requires  you to provide values for all columns in order , except\ncolumns with default values or AUTO_INCREMENT .\nNot recommended if your table structure might change (e.g., new columns\nadded later).\nInsert by Specifying Column Names (Best Practice)\nThis method is safer and more readable. You only insert into specific columns.\nor for multiple rows:INSERT INTO users VALUES\n(1,'Alice','alice@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1995-05-14' , DEFAULT );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Bob','bob@example.com' ,'Male','1990-11-23' );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES", 'Self JOIN in MySQL\nA Self JOIN  is a regular join, but the table is joined with itself .\nThis is useful when rows in the same table are related to each other. For example,\nwhen users refer other users, and we store the ID of the person who referred them\nin the same users table.\nStep 1: Add a referred_by_id  Column\nWe’ll extend the existing users table to include a column called referred_by_id ,\nwhich holds the id of the user who referred them.\nThis column:\nWill be NULL  for users who were not referred.\nWill contain the id of another user  who referred them.\nStep 2: Insert Referral Data (Optional)\nAssuming id = 1 is the first user, and referred others:ALTER TABLE users\nADD COLUMN referred_by_id INT ;\n• \n• \nUPDATE users SET referred_by_id =1 WHERE id IN (2,3);-- User 1 referred Users 2\nand3'] | How can I move a column to the first position of a table?                          | ["Altering a Table\nYou can use ALTER TABLE  to modify an existing table.\nAdd a Column\nDrop a Column\nModify a Column Type\nMove a Column to the First Position\nTo move a column (e.g., email) to the first position:\nTo move a column after another column (e.g., move gender after name):ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE ;\nALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN is_active ;\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (150);\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR (100) FIRST;\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other') AFTER name ;", 'Self JOIN in MySQL\nA Self JOIN  is a regular join, but the table is joined with itself .\nThis is useful when rows in the same table are related to each other. For example,\nwhen users refer other users, and we store the ID of the person who referred them\nin the same users table.\nStep 1: Add a referred_by_id  Column\nWe’ll extend the existing users table to include a column called referred_by_id ,\nwhich holds the id of the user who referred them.\nThis column:\nWill be NULL  for users who were not referred.\nWill contain the id of another user  who referred them.\nStep 2: Insert Referral Data (Optional)\nAssuming id = 1 is the first user, and referred others:ALTER TABLE users\nADD COLUMN referred_by_id INT ;\n• \n• \nUPDATE users SET referred_by_id =1 WHERE id IN (2,3);-- User 1 referred Users 2\nand3', "Inserting Data into MySQL Tables\nTo add data into a table, we use the INSERT INTO  statement.\nInsert Without Specifying Column Names (Full Row\nInsert)\nThis method requires  you to provide values for all columns in order , except\ncolumns with default values or AUTO_INCREMENT .\nNot recommended if your table structure might change (e.g., new columns\nadded later).\nInsert by Specifying Column Names (Best Practice)\nThis method is safer and more readable. | Why is it better to specify column names when inserting rows?                      | ["Inserting Data into MySQL Tables\nTo add data into a table, we use the INSERT INTO  statement.\nInsert Without Specifying Column Names (Full Row\nInsert)\nThis method requires  you to provide values for all columns in order , except\ncolumns with default values or AUTO_INCREMENT .\nNot recommended if your table structure might change (e.g., new columns\nadded later).\nInsert by Specifying Column Names (Best Practice)\nThis method is safer and more readable. You only insert into specific columns.\nor for multiple rows:INSERT INTO users VALUES\n(1,'Alice','alice@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1995-05-14' , DEFAULT );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Bob','bob@example.com' ,'Male','1990-11-23' );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES", "The remaining columns like id (which is AUTO_INCREMENT ) and created_at\n(which has a default) are automatically handled by MySQL.\nInsert Multiple Rows at Once\nThis is more efficient than inserting rows one by one.INSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Charlie' ,'charlie@example.com' ,'Other','1988-02-17' ),\n('David','david@example.com' ,'Male','2000-08-09' ),\n('Eva','eva@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1993-12-30' );", "Example:\nChange an existing column to NOT NULL:\nMake a column nullable again:\n3. CHECK Constraint\nEnsures that values in a column satisfy a specific condition .\nExample: Allow only dates of birth after Jan 1, 2000\nNaming the constraint ( chk_dob ) helps if you want to drop it later.\n4. DEFAULT  Constraint\nSets a default value  for a column if none is provided during insert.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100) NOT NULL\n);\nALTER TABLE users\nMODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (100) NOT NULL ;\nALTER TABLE users\nMODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (100) NULL;\nALTER TABLE users\nADD CONSTRAINT chk_dob CHECK (date_of_birth >'2000-01-01' );", 'Self JOIN in MySQL\nA Self JOIN  is a regular join, but the table is joined with itself .\nThis is useful when rows in the same table are related to each other. For example,\nwhen users refer other users, and we store the ID of the person who referred them\nin the same users table.\nStep 1: Add a referred_by_id  Column\nWe’ll extend the existing users table to include a column called referred_by_id ,\nwhich holds the id of the user who referred them.\nThis column:\nWill be NULL  for users who were not referred.\nWill contain the id of another user  who referred them.\nStep 2: Insert Referral Data (Optional)\nAssuming id = 1 is the first user, and referred others:ALTER TABLE users\nADD COLUMN referred_by_id INT ;\n• \n• \nUPDATE users SET referred_by_id =1 WHERE id IN (2,3);-- User 1 referred Users 2\nand3']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Specifying the column names in an INSERT statement is considered best practice because it makes the command **safer and more readable**. When you list the columns, you only need to supply values for the fields you actually want to set, and MySQL will handle any columns that have defaults or AUTO_INCREMENT values automatically. This also protects your code from breaking if the table’s structure changes later (e.g., new columns are added), since the INSERT won’t depend on a fixed column order. (Source: MySQL Handbook, page 10) | How do I select users whose name starts with the letter A?                         | ["IN\nLIKE (Pattern Matching)\nAND / OR\nORDER BY\nLIMITSELECT * FROM users WHERE gender IN ('Male','Other');\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'A%';-- Starts with A\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%a';-- Ends with a\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%li%';-- Contains 'li'\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE gender ='Female'  AND date_of_birth >'1990-01-01' ;\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE gender ='Male' OR gender ='Other';\nSELECT * FROM users ORDER BY date_of_birth ASC ;\nSELECT * FROM users ORDER BY name DESC ;\nSELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5;-- Top 5 rows\nSELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10 OFFSET 5;-- Skip first 5 rows, then get next10\nSELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5,10;-- Get 10 rows starting from the 6th row (Same as", "3. Wildcard Operators\nWildcards are used with the LIKE operator for pattern matching in text.\nWildcard Description Example\n%Matches any\nsequenceWHERE name LIKE 'A%'  (starts with A)\n_Matches a single\ncharacterWHERE name LIKE '_a%'  (second letter\nis ‘a’)\n4. LIMIT with OFFSET\nLIMIT is used to limit the number of rows returned. OFFSET skips a number of\nrows before starting to return rows.\nThis skips the first 10 rows and returns the next 5.\nAlternative syntax:\nThis also skips 10 and returns 5 (syntax: LIMIT offset, count ).\n5. DISTINCT Keyword\nDISTINCT  is used to return only unique values .SELECT * FROM users\nORDER BY id\nLIMIT 5 OFFSET 10;\nSELECT * FROM users\nORDER BY id\nLIMIT 10,5;", 'Step 3: Use a Self JOIN to Get Referrer Names\nWe want to get each user’s name along with the name of the person who referred\nthem .\nExplanation:\na refers to the user being queried.\nb refers to the user who referred them.\nLEFT JOIN  is used so that users with NULL in referred_by_id  are also\nincluded.\nSample Output:\nid user_name referred_by\n1 Aarav NULL\n2 Sneha Aarav\n3 Raj Aarav\n4 Fatima Sneha\nSummary\nUse Self JOIN  when you need to join a table with itself .\nIn referral-based relationships, store the referrer’s id in the same table.SELECT \n  a.id,\n  a.name AS user_name ,\n  b.name AS referred_by\nFROM users a\nINNER JOIN users b ON a .referred_by_id = b.id;\n• \n• \n• \n• \n• ', "Step 2: Insert Sample Data into admin_users\nStep 3: Use UNION to Combine Data\nLet’s combine the active and admin user names.\nThis returns a single list of unique names  from both tables.\nUNION ALL  Example\nIf you want to keep duplicate names (if any), use UNION ALL .\nUsing More Than One Column\nYou can also select multiple columns as long as both SELECT queries return the \nsame number of columns with compatible types .INSERT INTO admin_users (id, name, email, gender, date_of_birth , salary) VALUES\n(101,'Anil Kumar' ,'anil@example.com' ,'Male','1985-04-12' ,60000),\n(102,'Pooja Sharma' ,'pooja@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1992-09-20' ,58000),\n(103,'Rakesh Yadav' ,'rakesh@example.com' ,'Male','1989-11-05' ,54000),\n(104,'Fatima Begum' ,'fatima@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1990-06-30' ,62000);"] LEFT JOIN\nReturns all rows from the left table  (users), and matching rows from the right\ntable ( addresses ). | What happens if I run UPDATE without a WHERE clause?                               | ['This removes the table structure and all data  permanently.\nBest Practices\nAlways use WHERE unless you’re intentionally updating/deleting everything.\nConsider running a SELECT with the same WHERE clause first to confirm what\nwill be affected:\nAlways back up important data before performing destructive operations.\nQuick Quiz: Practice Your DELETE Skills\nwhat will happen if you run these queries?• \n• \nSELECT * FROM users WHERE id=3;\n• \nDELETE FROM users\nWHERE salary <50000;\nDELETE FROM users\nWHERE salary IS NULL ;', "UPDATE - Modifying Existing Data\nThe UPDATE statement is used to change values in one or more rows.\nBasic Syntax\nExample: Update One Column\nThis changes the name of the user with id = 1 to “Alicia”.\nExample: Update Multiple Columns\nWithout WHERE Clause (Warning)UPDATE table_name\nSET column1 = value1, column2 = value2\nWHERE condition ;\nUPDATE users\nSET name ='Alicia'\nWHERE id=1;\nUPDATE users\nSET name ='Robert' , email ='robert@example.com'\nWHERE id=2;\nUPDATE users\nSET gender ='Other';", "This updates every row  in the table. | What is the difference between DELETE FROM users and DROP TABLE users?             | ["DELETE - Removing Data from a Table\nThe DELETE statement removes rows from a table.\nBasic Syntax\nExample: Delete One Row\nDelete Multiple Rows\nDelete All Rows (but keep table structure)\nDrop the Entire Table (use with caution)DELETE FROM table_name\nWHERE condition ;\nDELETE FROM users\nWHERE id=3;\nDELETE FROM users\nWHERE gender ='Other';\nDELETE FROM users ;\nDROP TABLE users ;", "Step 2: Create a Table\nNow we’ll create a simple users table:\nThis table will store basic user info.\nStep 3: Drop the Database\nYou can delete the entire database (and all its tables) using:\nBe careful — this will delete everything in that database.\nData Types Explained\nINT: Integer type, used for whole numbers.\nVARCHAR(100) : Variable-length string, up to 100 characters.\nENUM: A string object with a value chosen from a list of permitted values. eg. \ngender ENUM('Male', 'Female', 'Other')\nDATE: Stores date values. eg date_of_birth DATECREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100) NOT NULL ,\n    email VARCHAR (100) UNIQUE NOT NULL ,\n    gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other'),\n    date_of_birth DATE ,\n    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP\n);", 'Returns a list of unique gender values from the users table.\n6. TRUNCATE Keyword\nTRUNCATE  removes all rows  from a table, but keeps the table structure .\nFaster than DELETE FROM users\nCannot be rolled back (unless in a transaction-safe environment)\n7. CHANGE vs MODIFY Column\nBoth CHANGE and MODIFY are used to alter existing columns in a table, but they\nwork slightly differently.\nCHANGE: Rename and change datatype\nThis renames city to location  and changes its type.\nMODIFY: Only change datatype\nThis changes only the datatype of salary.SELECT DISTINCT gender FROM users ;\nTRUNCATE TABLE users ;\n• \n• \nALTER TABLE users\nCHANGE COLUMN city location VARCHAR (150);\nALTER TABLE users\nMODIFY COLUMN salary BIGINT ;', 'But this may not  use the index effectively:\nBecause the first column in the index ( gender) is missing in the filter.\nDropping an Index\nTo delete an index:\nSummary\nFeature Description\nSHOW INDEXES View current indexes on a table\nCREATE INDEX Create single or multi-column indexes\nDROP INDEX Remove an index\nUse when Query performance on large tables is a concern\nAvoid on Columns that are rarely queried or always unique• \nWHERE salary >70000\nDROP INDEX idx_email ON users ;']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | `DELETE FROM users` removes rows from the **users** table but leaves the table itself (its definition, columns, indexes, etc.) intact. | How do I change an existing column so it cannot be NULL?                           | ["Example:\nChange an existing column to NOT NULL:\nMake a column nullable again:\n3. CHECK Constraint\nEnsures that values in a column satisfy a specific condition .\nExample: Allow only dates of birth after Jan 1, 2000\nNaming the constraint ( chk_dob ) helps if you want to drop it later.\n4. DEFAULT  Constraint\nSets a default value  for a column if none is provided during insert.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100) NOT NULL\n);\nALTER TABLE users\nMODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (100) NOT NULL ;\nALTER TABLE users\nMODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (100) NULL;\nALTER TABLE users\nADD CONSTRAINT chk_dob CHECK (date_of_birth >'2000-01-01' );", 'Self JOIN in MySQL\nA Self JOIN  is a regular join, but the table is joined with itself .\nThis is useful when rows in the same table are related to each other. For example,\nwhen users refer other users, and we store the ID of the person who referred them\nin the same users table.\nStep 1: Add a referred_by_id  Column\nWe’ll extend the existing users table to include a column called referred_by_id ,\nwhich holds the id of the user who referred them.\nThis column:\nWill be NULL  for users who were not referred.\nWill contain the id of another user  who referred them.\nStep 2: Insert Referral Data (Optional)\nAssuming id = 1 is the first user, and referred others:ALTER TABLE users\nADD COLUMN referred_by_id INT ;\n• \n• \nUPDATE users SET referred_by_id =1 WHERE id IN (2,3);-- User 1 referred Users 2\nand3', "Altering a Table\nYou can use ALTER TABLE  to modify an existing table.\nAdd a Column\nDrop a Column\nModify a Column Type\nMove a Column to the First Position\nTo move a column (e.g., email) to the first position:\nTo move a column after another column (e.g., move gender after name):ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE ;\nALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN is_active ;\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR (150);\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN email VARCHAR (100) FIRST;\nALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other') AFTER name ;", 'MySQL Constraints\nConstraints in MySQL are rules applied to table columns to ensure the accuracy , \nvalidity , and integrity  of the data.\n1. UNIQUE Constraint\nEnsures that all values in a column are different .\nExample (during table creation):\nAdd UNIQUE using ALTER TABLE :\n2. NOT NULL  Constraint\nEnsures that a column cannot contain NULL  values.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    email VARCHAR (100) UNIQUE\n);\nALTER TABLE users\nADD CONSTRAINT unique_email UNIQUE (email);']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | To make an existing column non‑nullable, use **ALTER TABLE** with **MODIFY COLUMN** and add the **NOT NULL** attribute.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | ALTER TABLE users MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL.                                                                             |       0.666667 |            0.833333 |

| Which MySQL function counts rows?                                                  | ["SQL Functions (MySQL)\nSQL functions help you analyze , transform , or summarize  data in your tables.\nWe’ll use the users table which includes:\nid, name, email, gender, date_of_birth , salary, created_at\n1. Aggregate Functions\nThese return a single value  from a set of rows.\nCOUNT()\nCount total number of users:\nCount users who are Female:\nMIN() and MAX()\nGet the minimum and maximum salary:• \nSELECT COUNT (*) FROM users ;\nSELECT COUNT (*) FROM users WHERE gender ='Female' ;\nSELECT MIN (salary) AS min_salary , MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM users ;", 'GROUP BY and HAVING in MySQL\nThe GROUP BY  clause is used to group rows that have the same values  in\nspecified columns. It is typically used with aggregate functions  like COUNT, SUM, \nAVG, MIN, or MAX.\nThe HAVING clause is used to filter groups  after aggregation — similar to how \nWHERE filters individual rows.\nExample Table: users\nAssume this is your users table:\nid name gender salary referred_by_id\n1 Aarav Male 80000 NULL\n2 Sneha Female 75000 1\n3 Raj Male 72000 1\n4 Fatima Female 85000 2\n5 Priya Female 70000 NULL\nGROUP BY Example: Average Salary by Gender\nSELECT gender , AVG(salary) AS average_salary\nFROM users\nGROUP BY gender ;', "The remaining columns like id (which is AUTO_INCREMENT ) and created_at\n(which has a default) are automatically handled by MySQL.\nInsert Multiple Rows at Once\nThis is more efficient than inserting rows one by one.INSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Charlie' ,'charlie@example.com' ,'Other','1988-02-17' ),\n('David','david@example.com' ,'Male','2000-08-09' ),\n('Eva','eva@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1993-12-30' );", "Querying Data in MySQL using SELECT\nThe SELECT statement is used to query data from a table.\nBasic Syntax\nTo select all columns:\nFiltering Rows with WHERE\nEqual To\nNot Equal ToSELECT column1 , column2 FROM table_name ;\nSELECT * FROM users ;\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE gender ='Male';\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE gender !='Female' ;\n--or\nSELECT * FROM users WHERE gender <>'Female' ;"]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | The MySQL function that counts rows is **`COUNT()`** (e.g., `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;`) (MySQL Handbook.pdf, page 25).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | COUNT(), e.g. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users.                                                                                               |       0.666667 |            1        |
| How can I calculate a user's age in years?                                         | ['DATEDIFF()\nFind number of days between today and birthdate:\nTIMESTAMPDIFF()\nCalculate age in years:\n4. Mathematical Functions\nROUND() , FLOOR() , CEIL()\nMOD()\nFind even or odd user IDs:SELECT name , DATEDIFF (CURDATE(), date_of_birth ) AS days_lived FROM users ;\nSELECT name , TIMESTAMPDIFF (YEAR, date_of_birth , CURDATE ()) AS age FROM users ;\nSELECT salary ,\n       ROUND (salary) AS rounded ,\n       FLOOR (salary) AS floored ,\n       CEIL (salary) AS ceiled\nFROM users ;\nSELECT id, MOD(id,2) AS remainder FROM users ;', 'Explanation:\nThis groups users by gender.\nThen calculates the average salary for each group.\nGROUP BY with COUNT\nFind how many users were referred by each user:\nOutput:\nreferred_by_id total_referred\n1 2\n2 1\nHAVING Clause: Filtering Groups\nLet’s say we only want to show genders where the average salary is greater than\n₹75,000 .• \n• \nSELECT referred_by_id , COUNT(*) AS total_referred\nFROM users\nWHERE referred_by_id IS NOT NULL\nGROUP BY referred_by_id ;\nSELECT gender , AVG(salary) AS avg_salary\nFROM users\nGROUP BY gender\nHAVING AVG (salary)>75000;', "5. Conditional Functions\nIF()\nSummary Table\nFunction Purpose\nCOUNT() Count rows\nSUM() Total of a column\nAVG() Average of values\nMIN()/MAX() Lowest / highest value\nLENGTH() String length\nCONCAT() Merge strings\nYEAR()/DATEDIFF() Date breakdown / age\nROUND() Rounding numbers\nIF() Conditional logicSELECT name , gender,\n       IF (gender ='Female' ,'Yes','No') AS is_female\nFROM users ;", 'Explanation:\nThis will give you a count of users by gender, along with a grand total for all\nusers.SELECT gender , COUNT(*) AS total_users\nFROM users\nGROUP BY gender WITH ROLLUP ;\n• '] | How do I combine a name and an email into a single string?                         | ["Step 2: Insert Sample Data into admin_users\nStep 3: Use UNION to Combine Data\nLet’s combine the active and admin user names.\nThis returns a single list of unique names  from both tables.\nUNION ALL  Example\nIf you want to keep duplicate names (if any), use UNION ALL .\nUsing More Than One Column\nYou can also select multiple columns as long as both SELECT queries return the \nsame number of columns with compatible types .INSERT INTO admin_users (id, name, email, gender, date_of_birth , salary) VALUES\n(101,'Anil Kumar' ,'anil@example.com' ,'Male','1985-04-12' ,60000),\n(102,'Pooja Sharma' ,'pooja@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1992-09-20' ,58000),\n(103,'Rakesh Yadav' ,'rakesh@example.com' ,'Male','1989-11-05' ,54000),\n(104,'Fatima Begum' ,'fatima@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1990-06-30' ,62000);", "SQL UNION and UNION ALL\nThe UNION operator in SQL is used to combine the result sets of two or more \nSELECT statements . It removes duplicates by default.\nIf you want to include all rows including duplicates, use UNION ALL .\nExample Scenario\nYou already have a users table for active users. Now, we’ll create an \nadmin_users  table to store users who are administrators or have special roles. We\nwill then combine the names from both tables using UNION.\nStep 1: Create the admin_users  Table\nCREATE TABLE admin_users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100),\n    email VARCHAR (100),\n    gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other'),\n    date_of_birth DATE ,\n    salary INT\n);", "LOWER()  and UPPER()\nConvert names to lowercase or uppercase:\nCONCAT()\nCombine name and email:\n3. Date Functions\nNOW()\nCurrent date and time:\nYEAR(), MONTH() , DAY()\nExtract parts of date_of_birth :SELECT name , LOWER(name) AS lowercase_name FROM users ;\nSELECT name , UPPER(name) AS uppercase_name FROM users ;\nSELECT CONCAT (name,' <', email,'>') AS user_contact FROM users ;\nSELECT NOW ();\nSELECT name , YEAR(date_of_birth ) AS birth_year FROM users ;", "The remaining columns like id (which is AUTO_INCREMENT ) and created_at\n(which has a default) are automatically handled by MySQL.\nInsert Multiple Rows at Once\nThis is more efficient than inserting rows one by one.INSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Charlie' ,'charlie@example.com' ,'Other','1988-02-17' ),\n('David','david@example.com' ,'Male','2000-08-09' ),\n('Eva','eva@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1993-12-30' );"]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Use MySQL’s `CONCAT()` function to join the two fields. For example:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Use CONCAT(), e.g. CONCAT(name, ' <', email, '>').                                                                                      |     nan        |          nan        |

| What is the default mode for transactions in MySQL and how do I turn it off?       | ['MySQL Transactions and AutoCommit\nBy default, MySQL operates in AutoCommit  mode. This means that every SQL\nstatement is treated as a transaction  and is committed automatically. However, for\nmore control over when changes are saved, you can turn AutoCommit  off and\nmanage transactions manually.\n1. Disabling AutoCommit\nWhen AutoCommit  is off, you can explicitly control when to commit or rollback\nchanges.\nTo disable AutoCommit:\nThis turns off AutoCommit, meaning that changes you make won’t be saved to the\ndatabase unless you explicitly tell MySQL to commit them.\nImportant : Until you execute a COMMIT, your changes are not permanent.\n2. COMMIT — Save Changes to the Database\nOnce you’ve made changes and you’re confident that everything is correct, you can', 'Adding ON DELETE  Action\nBy default, if you delete a user that has related addresses, MySQL will throw an\nerror. It’s useful\nwhen you want to encapsulate logic that can be reused multiple times — like\nqueries, updates, or conditional operations.\nWhy Change the Delimiter?\nBy default, MySQL uses ; to end SQL statements.\nBut when defining stored procedures, we use ;inside  the procedure as well. | How is a PRIMARY KEY different from a UNIQUE constraint?                           | ['Understanding PRIMARY KEY  in MySQL\nA PRIMARY KEY  is a constraint in SQL that uniquely identifies each row  in a table.\nIt is one of the most important concepts in database design.\nWhat is a Primary Key?\nA PRIMARY KEY :\nMust be unique\nCannot be NULL\nIs used to identify rows in a table\nCan be a single column or a combination of columns\nEach table can have only one  primary key\nExample:\nHow Is PRIMARY KEY  Different from UNIQUE?\nAt first glance, PRIMARY KEY  and UNIQUE might seem similar since both prevent\nduplicate values. But there are important differences:• \n• \n• \n• \n• \n• \nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100)\n);', 'This may fail if the primary key is being used elsewhere (like in a foreign key\nor auto_increment column).\nTo drop a UNIQUE constraint:\nAuto Increment\nIn MySQL, a PRIMARY KEY  is often used with the AUTO_INCREMENT  attribute to\nautomatically generate unique values for new rows.\nThis means that every time you insert a new row, MySQL will automatically assign a\nunique value to the id column. You can change the starting value of \nAUTO_INCREMENT  using:\nKey Takeaways\nUse PRIMARY KEY  for the main identifier  of a row.\nUse UNIQUE for enforcing non-duplicate values  in other columns (like email\nor phone).\nYou can have only one primary key , but you can have many unique\nconstraints .ALTER TABLE users DROP INDEX email ;\nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,', 'Feature PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE\nMust be\nuniqueYes Yes\nAllows NULL\nvaluesNoYes (one or more NULLs\nallowed)\nHow many\nallowedOnly one per table Can have multiple\nRequired by\ntableRecommended, often\nrequiredOptional\nDropping Cannot be easily dropped Can be dropped anytime\nExample with UNIQUE\nIn this example:\nid is the unique identifier for each row.\nemail must be unique, but is not the primary key.\nCan I Drop a PRIMARY KEY?\nYes, but it is more restricted than dropping a UNIQUE constraint.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    email VARCHAR (100) UNIQUE,\n    name VARCHAR (100)\n);\n• \n• \nALTER TABLE users DROP PRIMARY KEY ;', 'Example:\nAdd DEFAULT using ALTER TABLE :\n5. PRIMARY KEY  Constraint\nUniquely identifies each row. Must be NOT NULL  and UNIQUE .\nExample:\nAdd later with ALTER TABLE :\n6. AUTO_INCREMENT\nUsed with PRIMARY KEY  to automatically assign the next number.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    is_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE\n);\nALTER TABLE users\nALTER COLUMN is_active SET DEFAULT TRUE ;\nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100)\n);\nALTER TABLE users\nADD PRIMARY KEY (id);']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | A PRIMARY KEY and a UNIQUE constraint both enforce uniqueness, but they differ in several important ways:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | A table can have only one primary key, which cannot be NULL; UNIQUE can be used on several columns and allows NULLs.                    |     nan        |          nan        |

| How do I drop a UNIQUE constraint on the email column?                             | ['This may fail if the primary key is being used elsewhere (like in a foreign key\nor auto_increment column).\nTo drop a UNIQUE constraint:\nAuto Increment\nIn MySQL, a PRIMARY KEY  is often used with the AUTO_INCREMENT  attribute to\nautomatically generate unique values for new rows.\nThis means that every time you insert a new row, MySQL will automatically assign a\nunique value to the id column. You can change the starting value of \nAUTO_INCREMENT  using:\nKey Takeaways\nUse PRIMARY KEY  for the main identifier  of a row.\nUse UNIQUE for enforcing non-duplicate values  in other columns (like email\nor phone).\nYou can have only one primary key , but you can have many unique\nconstraints .ALTER TABLE users DROP INDEX email ;\nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,', 'Feature PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE\nMust be\nuniqueYes Yes\nAllows NULL\nvaluesNoYes (one or more NULLs\nallowed)\nHow many\nallowedOnly one per table Can have multiple\nRequired by\ntableRecommended, often\nrequiredOptional\nDropping Cannot be easily dropped Can be dropped anytime\nExample with UNIQUE\nIn this example:\nid is the unique identifier for each row.\nemail must be unique, but is not the primary key.\nCan I Drop a PRIMARY KEY?\nYes, but it is more restricted than dropping a UNIQUE constraint.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    email VARCHAR (100) UNIQUE,\n    name VARCHAR (100)\n);\n• \n• \nALTER TABLE users DROP PRIMARY KEY ;', 'e many unique\nconstraints .ALTER TABLE users DROP INDEX email ;\nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,     name VARCHAR (100)\n);\nALTER TABLE users AUTO_INCREMENT =1000;\n• \n• \n•', 'MySQL Constraints\nConstraints in MySQL are rules applied to table columns to ensure the accuracy , \nvalidity , and integrity  of the data.\n1. UNIQUE Constraint\nEnsures that all values in a column are different .\nExample (during table creation):\nAdd UNIQUE using ALTER TABLE :\n2. NOT NULL  Constraint\nEnsures that a column cannot contain NULL  values.CREATE TABLE users (\nid INT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    email VARCHAR (100) UNIQUE\n);\nALTER TABLE users\nADD CONSTRAINT unique_email UNIQUE (email);'] | How do I change the starting value of AUTO_INCREMENT?                              | ['This may fail if the primary key is being used elsewhere (like in a foreign key\nor auto_increment column).\nTo drop a UNIQUE constraint:\nAuto Increment\nIn MySQL, a PRIMARY KEY  is often used with the AUTO_INCREMENT  attribute to\nautomatically generate unique values for new rows.\nThis means that every time you insert a new row, MySQL will automatically assign a\nunique value to the id column. You can change the starting value of \nAUTO_INCREMENT  using:\nKey Takeaways\nUse PRIMARY KEY  for the main identifier  of a row.\nUse UNIQUE for enforcing non-duplicate values  in other columns (like email\nor phone).\nYou can have only one primary key , but you can have many unique\nconstraints .ALTER TABLE users DROP INDEX email ;\nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,', "The remaining columns like id (which is AUTO_INCREMENT ) and created_at\n(which has a default) are automatically handled by MySQL.\nInsert Multiple Rows at Once\nThis is more efficient than inserting rows one by one.INSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Charlie' ,'charlie@example.com' ,'Other','1988-02-17' ),\n('David','david@example.com' ,'Male','2000-08-09' ),\n('Eva','eva@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1993-12-30' );", "Inserting Data into MySQL Tables\nTo add data into a table, we use the INSERT INTO  statement.\nInsert Without Specifying Column Names (Full Row\nInsert)\nThis method requires  you to provide values for all columns in order , except\ncolumns with default values or AUTO_INCREMENT .\nNot recommended if your table structure might change (e.g., new columns\nadded later).\nInsert by Specifying Column Names (Best Practice)\nThis method is safer and more readable. You only insert into specific columns.\nor for multiple rows:INSERT INTO users VALUES\n(1,'Alice','alice@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1995-05-14' , DEFAULT );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Bob','bob@example.com' ,'Male','1990-11-23' );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES", 'Example:\nEach new row gets the next available integer value in id.\nSummary Table\nConstraint Purpose\nUNIQUE Prevents duplicate values\nNOT NULL Ensures value is not NULL\nCHECK Restricts values using a condition\nDEFAULT Sets a default value\nPRIMARY KEY Uniquely identifies each row\nAUTO_INCREMENT Automatically generates unique numbersCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100)\n);']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | You can change the starting value of an AUTO_INCREMENT column by issuing an ALTER TABLE statement that sets a new AUTO_INCREMENT value. For example:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | ALTER TABLE users AUTO_INCREMENT = 1000.                                                                                                |     nan        |          nan        |

| How do I create a foreign key that links addresses to users?                       | ['Foreign Keys in MySQL\nA foreign key  is a column that creates a link between two tables . It ensures that\nthe value in one table must match  a value in another table.\nThis is used to maintain data integrity  between related data.\nWhy Use Foreign Keys?\nImagine this scenario:\nYou have a users table. Now you want to store each user’s address. Instead of\nputting address columns inside the users table, you create a separate \naddresses  table, and link it to users using a foreign key .\nCreating a Table with a Foreign Key\nLet’s create an addresses  table where each address belongs to a user.\nCREATE TABLE addresses (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    user_id INT ,\n    street VARCHAR (255),\n    city VARCHAR (100),\n    state VARCHAR (100),\n    pincode VARCHAR (10),', 'Explanation:\nuser_id  is a foreign key .\nIt references the id column in the users table.\nThis ensures that every address must be linked to a valid user.\nDropping a Foreign Key\nTo drop a foreign key, you need to know its constraint name . MySQL auto-\ngenerates it if you don’t specify one, or you can name it yourself:\nTo drop it:\nAdding a Foreign Key Later (Using ALTER)\nSuppose the foreign key was not defined during table creation . You can add it\nlater using ALTER TABLE :• \n• \n• \nCREATE TABLE addresses (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    user_id INT ,\n    CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id)\n);\nALTER TABLE addresses\nDROP FOREIGN KEY fk_user ;\nALTER TABLE addresses\nADD CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id);', 'Summary\nForeign keys connect tables  and enforce valid references .\nYou can create them inline or with ALTER TABLE .\nYou can drop them by name.\nUse ON DELETE  to control what happens when the parent row is deleted.• \n• \n• \n• ', 'SQL JOINs in MySQL\nIn SQL, JOINs  are used to combine rows from two or more tables  based on related\ncolumns — usually a foreign key  in one table referencing a primary key  in another.\nWe’ll use the following two tables:\nusers table\nid name\n1 Aarav\n2 Sneha\n3 Raj\naddresses  table\nid user_id city\n1 1 Mumbai\n2 2 Kolkata\n3 4 Delhi\nNote: user_id  is a foreign key  that references users.id .\n1. INNER JOIN\nReturns only the matching rows  from both tables.']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | To link the **addresses** table to the **users** table you define a foreign‑key column (e.g., `user_id`) that references the primary‑key column (`id`) in **users**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Add FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) in the addresses table.                                                                  |     nan        |          nan        |

Options\nON\xa0DELETE\nOptionBehavior\nCASCADE Deletes all related rows in child table\nSET NULL Sets the foreign key to NULL in the child table\nRESTRICT Prevents deletion of parent if child exists (default)CREATE TABLE addresses (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    user_id INT ,\n    street VARCHAR (255),\n    city VARCHAR (100),\n    state VARCHAR (100),\n    pincode VARCHAR (10),\n    CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n);\nALTER TABLE addresses', 'CHAR (10),\n    CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n);\nALTER TABLE addresses ADD CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE \nCASCADE;', "DELETE - Removing Data from a Table\nThe DELETE statement removes rows from a table.\nBasic Syntax\nExample: Delete One Row\nDelete Multiple Rows\nDelete All Rows (but keep table structure)\nDrop the Entire Table (use with caution)DELETE FROM table_name\nWHERE condition ;\nDELETE FROM users\nWHERE id=3;\nDELETE FROM users\nWHERE gender ='Other';\nDELETE FROM users ;\nDROP TABLE users ;", 'This removes the table structure and all data  permanently.\nBest                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | ON DELETE CASCADE causes MySQL to automatically delete any rows in the child table that reference the parent row being removed. In other words, when a parent record (e.g., a user) is deleted, all related child records (e.g., that user’s addresses) are deleted as well (source, page 38).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | It automatically deletes the related rows in the child table when the parent row is deleted.                                            |     nan        |          nan        |
| What is the default ON DELETE behavior of a foreign key?                           | ['Adding ON DELETE  Action\nBy default, if you delete a user that has related addresses, MySQL will throw an\nerror. You can control this behavior with ON DELETE .\nExample with ON DELETE CASCADE :\nIf you want addresses to be automatically deleted when the user is deleted:\nOr alter it later:\nOther ON DELETE Options\nON\xa0DELETE\nOptionBehavior\nCASCADE Deletes all related rows in child table\nSET NULL Sets the foreign key to NULL in the child table\nRESTRICT Prevents deletion of parent if child exists (default)CREATE TABLE addresses (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    user_id INT ,\n    street VARCHAR (255),\n    city VARCHAR (100),\n    state VARCHAR (100),\n    pincode VARCHAR (10),\n    CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n);\nALTER TABLE addresses', 'Summary\nForeign keys connect tables  and enforce valid references .\nYou can create them inline or with ALTER TABLE .\nYou can drop them by name.\nUse ON DELETE  to control what happens when the parent row is deleted.• \n• \n• \n• ', 'CHAR (10),\n    CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE\n);\nALTER TABLE addresses ADD CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE \nCASCADE;', 'Explanation:\nuser_id  is a foreign key .\nIt references the id column in the users table.\nThis ensures that every address must be linked to a valid user.\nDropping a Foreign Key\nTo drop a foreign key, you need to know its constraint name . MySQL auto-\ngenerates it if you don’t specify one, or you can name it yourself:\nTo drop it:\nAdding a Foreign Key Later (Using ALTER)\nSuppose the foreign key was not defined during table creation . You can add it\nlater using ALTER TABLE :• \n• \n• \nCREATE TABLE addresses (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    user_id INT ,\n    CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id)\n);\nALTER TABLE addresses\nDROP FOREIGN KEY fk_user ;\nALTER TABLE addresses\nADD CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users (id);']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | The default ON DELETE behavior for a foreign key is **RESTRICT** – it prevents the parent row from being deleted while related child rows exist (the default setting). | What does an INNER JOIN return?                                                    | ['SQL JOINs in MySQL\nIn SQL, JOINs  are used to combine rows from two or more tables  based on related\ncolumns — usually a foreign key  in one table referencing a primary key  in another.\nWe’ll use the following two tables:\nusers table\nid name\n1 Aarav\n2 Sneha\n3 Raj\naddresses  table\nid user_id city\n1 1 Mumbai\n2 2 Kolkata\n3 4 Delhi\nNote: user_id  is a foreign key  that references users.id .\n1. INNER JOIN\nReturns only the matching rows  from both tables.', 'Output:\nname city\nAarav Mumbai\nSneha Kolkata\nRaj is excluded because there is no matching address. Delhi is excluded\nbecause its user_id  (4) is not in users.\nVisual Representation:\n2. LEFT JOIN\nReturns all rows from the left table  (users), and matching rows from the right\ntable ( addresses ). If no match is found, NULLs are returned.SELECT users .name, addresses .city\nFROM users\nINNER JOIN addresses ON users .id= addresses .user_id;\nusers          addresses\n----- ------\n|1| |1|\n|2| |2|\n|| ||\n=> only matching pairs\nSELECT users .name, addresses .city\nFROM users\nLEFT JOIN addresses ON users .id= addresses .user_id;', 'name city\nNULL Delhi\nDelhi is shown even though it points to a user_id  that doesn’t exist.\nVisual Representation:\nSummary Table\nJOIN Type Description\nINNER JOIN Only matching rows from both tables\nLEFT JOIN All rows from left table + matching from right\nRIGHT JOIN All rows from right table + matching from leftusers          addresses\n----- ------\n|1| |1|\n|2| |2|\n|| |4|\n=>all addresses + matched users (or NULL)', 'Step 3: Use a Self JOIN to Get Referrer Names\nWe want to get each user’s name along with the name of the person who referred\nthem .\nExplanation:\na refers to the user being queried.\nb refers to the user who referred them.\nLEFT JOIN  is used so that users with NULL in referred_by_id  are also\nincluded.\nSample Output:\nid user_name referred_by\n1 Aarav NULL\n2 Sneha Aarav\n3 Raj Aarav\n4 Fatima Sneha\nSummary\nUse Self JOIN  when you need to join a table with itself .\nIn referral-based relationships, store the referrer’s id in the same table.SELECT \n  a.id,\n  a.name AS user_name ,\n  b.name AS referred_by\nFROM users a\nINNER JOIN users b ON a .referred_by_id = b.id;\n• \n• \n• \n• \n• '] only the matching rows from both tables). (MySQL Handbook.pdf, page 40)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Only the rows that match in both tables.                                                                                                |     nan        |          nan        |

| What is a Self JOIN and when is it used?                                           | ['Self JOIN in MySQL\nA Self JOIN  is a regular join, but the table is joined with itself .\nThis is useful when rows in the same table are related to each other. For example,\nwhen users refer other users, and we store the ID of the person who referred them\nin the same users table.\nStep 1: Add a referred_by_id  Column\nWe’ll extend the existing users table to include a column called referred_by_id ,\nwhich holds the id of the user who referred them.\nThis column:\nWill be NULL  for users who were not referred.\nWill contain the id of another user  who referred them.\nStep 2: Insert Referral Data (Optional)\nAssuming id = 1 is the first user, and referred others:ALTER TABLE users\nADD COLUMN referred_by_id INT ;\n• \n• \nUPDATE users SET referred_by_id =1 WHERE id IN (2,3);-- User 1 referred Users 2\nand3', 'Step 3: Use a Self JOIN to Get Referrer Names\nWe want to get each user’s name along with the name of the person who referred\nthem .\nExplanation:\na refers to the user being queried.\nb refers to the user who referred them.\nLEFT JOIN  is used so that users with NULL in referred_by_id  are also\nincluded.\nSample Output:\nid user_name referred_by\n1 Aarav NULL\n2 Sneha Aarav\n3 Raj Aarav\n4 Fatima Sneha\nSummary\nUse Self JOIN  when you need to join a table with itself .\nIn referral-based relationships, store the referrer’s id in the same table.SELECT \n  a.id,\n  a.name AS user_name ,\n  b.name AS referred_by\nFROM users a\nINNER JOIN users b ON a .referred_by_id = b.id;\n• \n• \n• \n• \n• ', 'SQL JOINs in MySQL\nIn SQL, JOINs  are used to combine rows from two or more tables  based on related\ncolumns — usually a foreign key  in one table referencing a primary key  in another.\nWe’ll use the following two tables:\nusers table\nid name\n1 Aarav\n2 Sneha\n3 Raj\naddresses  table\nid user_id city\n1 1 Mumbai\n2 2 Kolkata\n3 4 Delhi\nNote: user_id  is a foreign key  that references users.id .\n1. | Does a MySQL view store its own data?                                              | ['MySQL Views\nA view in MySQL is a virtual table  based on the result of a SELECT query. It does\nnot store data itself — it always reflects the current data  in the base tables.\nViews are useful when:\nYou want to simplify complex queries\nYou want to reuse logic\nYou want to hide certain columns from users\nYou want a “live snapshot” of filtered data\nCreating a View\nSuppose we want a view that lists all users earning more than ₹70,000.\nQuerying the View\nThis will return all users from the users table where salary is above ₹70,000.• \n• \n• \n• \nCREATE VIEW high_salary_users AS\nSELECT id, name, salary\nFROM users\nWHERE salary >70000;\nSELECT * FROM high_salary_users ;', 'Getting Started with MySQL\nWhat is a Database?\nA database  is a container that stores related data in an organized way. | How do I see which indexes exist on a table?                                       | ["MySQL Indexes\nIndexes in MySQL are used to speed up data retrieval . They work like the index of\na book — helping the database engine find rows faster, especially for searches,\nfilters, and joins .\nViewing Indexes on a Table\nTo see the indexes on a table, use:\nThis shows all the indexes currently defined on the users table, including the\nautomatically created primary key  index.\nCreating a Single-Column Index\nSuppose you’re frequently searching users by their email. You can speed this up\nby indexing the email column.\nWhat this does:\nCreates an index named idx_email\nImproves performance of queries like:SHOW INDEXES FROM users ;\nCREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);\n• \n• \nSELECT * FROM users WHERE email ='example@example.com' ;", 'But this may not  use the index effectively:\nBecause the first column in the index ( gender) is missing in the filter.\nDropping an Index\nTo delete an index:\nSummary\nFeature Description\nSHOW INDEXES View current indexes on a table\nCREATE INDEX Create single or multi-column indexes\nDROP INDEX Remove an index\nUse when Query performance on large tables is a concern\nAvoid on Columns that are rarely queried or always unique• \nWHERE salary >70000\nDROP INDEX idx_email ON users ;', "Important Notes\nIndexes consume extra disk space\nIndexes slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations slightly\n(because the index must be updated)\nUse indexes only when needed  (i.e., for columns used in | Why does the order of columns matter in a multi-column index?                      | ["Important Notes\nIndexes consume extra disk space\nIndexes slow down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations slightly\n(because the index must be updated)\nUse indexes only when needed  (i.e., for columns used in WHERE, JOIN, \nORDER BY )\nCreating a Multi-Column Index\nIf you often query users using both gender and salary, a multi-column index is\nmore efficient than separate indexes.\nUsage Example:\nThis query can take advantage of the combined index on gender and salary.\nIndex Order Matters\nFor a multi-column index on (gender, salary) :\nThis works efficiently:• \n• \n• \nCREATE INDEX idx_gender_salary ON users (gender, salary);\nSELECT * FROM users\nWHERE gender ='Female'  AND salary >70000;\n• \nWHERE gender ='Female'  AND salary >70000", 'But this may not  use the index effectively:\nBecause the first column in the index ( gender) is missing in the filter.\nDropping an Index\nTo delete an index:\nSummary\nFeature Description\nSHOW INDEXES View current indexes on a table\nCREATE INDEX Create single or multi-column indexes\nDROP INDEX Remove an index\nUse when Query performance on large tables is a concern\nAvoid on Columns that are rarely queried or always unique• \nWHERE salary >70000\nDROP INDEX idx_email ON users ;', "MySQL Indexes\nIndexes in MySQL are used to speed up data retrieval . They work like the index of\na book — helping the database engine find rows faster, especially for searches,\nfilters, and joins .\nViewing Indexes on a Table\nTo see the indexes on a table, use:\nThis shows all the indexes currently defined on the users table, including the\nautomatically created primary key  index.\nCreating a Single-Column Index\nSuppose you’re frequently searching users by their email. You can speed this up\nby indexing the email column.\nWhat this does:\nCreates an index named idx_email\nImproves performance of queries like:SHOW INDEXES FROM users ;\nCREATE INDEX idx_email ON users (email);\n• \n• \nSELECT * FROM users WHERE email ='example@example.com' ;", "Inserting Data into MySQL Tables\nTo add data into a table, we use the INSERT INTO  statement.\nInsert Without Specifying Column Names (Full Row\nInsert)\nThis method requires  you to provide values for all columns in order , except\ncolumns with default values or AUTO_INCREMENT .\nNot recommended if your table structure might change (e.g., new columns\nadded later).\nInsert by Specifying Column Names (Best Practice)\nThis method is safer and more readable. You only insert into specific columns.\nor for multiple rows:INSERT INTO users VALUES\n(1,'Alice','alice@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1995-05-14' , DEFAULT );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES\n('Bob','bob@example.com' ,'Male','1990-11-23' );\nINSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth ) VALUES"]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | The order of the columns in a multi‑column index determines how MySQL can use that index. | How do I find users who earn more than the average salary?                         | ['The outer query selects all users with a salary greater than that average .\nSubquery with IN\nNow let’s say we want to find users who have been referred by someone who earns\nmore than ₹75,000.\nExplanation:\nThe inner query: SELECT id FROM users WHERE salary > 75000  returns a list\nof user IDs (referrers) who earn more than ₹75,000.\nThe outer query selects users whose referred_by_id  is in that list.\nOther Places Subqueries Are Used\nYou can also use subqueries:\nInside SELECT columns (called scalar subqueries)\nIn the FROM clause to create derived tables\nExample in SELECT:\nThis shows each user’s salary along with the overall average.• \nSELECT id, name, referred_by_id\nFROM users\nWHERE referred_by_id IN (\n    SELECT id FROM users WHERE salary >75000\n);\n• \n• \n• \n• \nSELECT name , salary,', 'Subqueries in MySQL\nA subquery  is a query nested inside another query. Subqueries are useful for\nbreaking down complex problems into smaller parts.\nThey can be used in:\nSELECT statements\nWHERE clauses\nFROM clauses\nExample Scenario: Salary Comparison\nSuppose we want to find all users who earn more than the average salary  of all\nusers.\nScalar Subquery Example\nThis subquery returns a single value  — the average salary — and we compare each\nuser’s salary against it.\nExplanation:\nThe inner query: SELECT AVG(salary) FROM users  returns the average salary.• \n• \n• \nSELECT id, name, salary\nFROM users\nWHERE salary >(\n    SELECT AVG (salary) FROM users\n);\n• ', 'Explanation:\nThis groups users by gender.\nThen calculates the average salary for each group.\nGROUP BY with COUNT\nFind how many users were referred by each user:\nOutput:\nreferred_by_id total_referred\n1 2\n2 1\nHAVING Clause: Filtering Groups\nLet’s say we only want to show genders where the average salary is greater than\n₹75,000 .• \n• \nSELECT referred_by_id , COUNT(*) AS total_referred\nFROM users\nWHERE referred_by_id IS NOT NULL\nGROUP BY referred_by_id ;\nSELECT gender , AVG(salary) AS avg_salary\nFROM users\nGROUP BY gender\nHAVING AVG (salary)>75000;', 'MySQL Views\nA view in MySQL is a virtual table  based on the result of a SELECT query. It does\nnot store data itself — it always reflects the current data  in the base tables.\nViews are useful when:\nYou want to simplify complex queries\nYou want to reuse logic\nYou want to hide certain columns from users\nYou want a “live snapshot” of filtered data\nCreating a View\nSuppose we want a view that lists all users earning more than ₹70,000.\nQuerying the View\nThis will return all users from the users table where salary is above ₹70,000.• \n• \n• \n• \nCREATE VIEW high_salary_users AS\nSELECT id, name, salary\nFROM users\nWHERE salary >70000;\nSELECT * FROM high_salary_users ;'] | What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?                                   | ['Why not WHERE?\nWHERE is used before  grouping.\nHAVING is used after  groups are formed — it’s the only way to filter\naggregated values.\nAnother Example: Groups with More Than 1 Referral\nSummary\nClause PurposeCan use\naggregates?\nWHERE Filters rows before  grouping No\nGROUP \nBYGroups rows based on column values N/A\nHAVING Filters groups after  aggregation Yes\nUse GROUP BY  to organize data, and HAVING to filter those groups based on\naggregate conditions.\nROLLUP\nTo get subtotals and grand totals, you can use ROLLUP:• \n• \nSELECT referred_by_id , COUNT(*) AS total_referred\nFROM users\nWHERE referred_by_id IS NOT NULL\nGROUP BY referred_by_id\nHAVING COUNT (*)>1;', 'GROUP BY and HAVING in MySQL\nThe GROUP BY  clause is used to group rows that have the same values  in\nspecified columns. It is typically used with aggregate functions  like COUNT, SUM, \nAVG, MIN, or MAX.\nThe HAVING clause is used to filter groups  after aggregation — similar to how \nWHERE filters individual rows.\nExample Table: users\nAssume this is your users table:\nid name gender salary referred_by_id\n1 Aarav Male 80000 NULL\n2 Sneha Female 75000 1\n3 Raj Male 72000 1\n4 Fatima Female 85000 2\n5 Priya Female 70000 NULL\nGROUP BY Example: Average Salary by Gender\nSELECT gender , AVG(salary) AS average_salary\nFROM users\nGROUP BY gender ;', 'Understanding PRIMARY KEY  in MySQL\nA PRIMARY KEY  is a constraint in SQL that uniquely identifies each row  in a table.\nIt is one of the most important concepts in database design.\nWhat is a Primary Key?\nA PRIMARY KEY :\nMust be unique\nCannot be NULL\nIs used to identify rows in a table\nCan be a single column or a combination of columns\nEach table can have only one  primary key\nExample:\nHow Is PRIMARY KEY  Different from UNIQUE?\nAt first glance, PRIMARY KEY  and UNIQUE might seem similar since both prevent\nduplicate values. But there are important differences:• \n• \n• \n• \n• \n• \nCREATE TABLE users (\nid INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY ,\n    name VARCHAR (100)\n);', 'Getting Started with MySQL\nWhat is a Database?\nA database  is a container that stores related data in an organized way. In MySQL, a\ndatabase holds one or more tables .\nThink of it like:\nFolder analogy :\nA database  is like a folder.\nEach table  is a file inside that folder.\nThe rows  in the table are like the content inside each file.\nExcel analogy :\nA database  is like an Excel workbook.\nEach table  is a separate sheet inside that workbook.\nEach row in the table is like a row in Excel.\nStep 1: Create a Database\nAfter creating the database, either:\nRight-click it in MySQL Workbench and select “Set as Default Schema” , or\nUse this SQL command:• \n• \n• \n• \n• \n• \n• \n• \nCREATE DATABASE startersql ;\n• \n• \nUSE startersql ;']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | **WHERE** and **HAVING** serve different filtering stages in a query:                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | WHERE filters rows before grouping; | Why must I change the DELIMITER when creating a stored procedure?                  | ['Stored Procedures in MySQL\nA stored procedure  is a saved SQL block that can be executed later. It’s useful\nwhen you want to encapsulate logic that can be reused multiple times — like\nqueries, updates, or conditional operations.\nWhy Change the Delimiter?\nBy default, MySQL uses ; to end SQL statements.\nBut when defining stored procedures, we use ;inside  the procedure as well. This\ncan confuse MySQL. To avoid this, we temporarily change the delimiter  (e.g.\xa0to \n$$ or //) while creating the procedure.\nSyntax for Creating a Stored Procedure\nAfter the procedure is created, we reset the delimiter back to ;.DELIMITER $$\nCREATE PROCEDURE procedure_name ()\nBEGIN\n-- SQL statements go here\nEND$$\nDELIMITER ;', "Notes\nInput parameters are declared using the IN keyword.\nStored procedures are stored in the database and can be reused.\nViewing Stored Procedures\nDropping a Stored Procedure\nSummary\nCommand Purpose\nDELIMITER $$ Temporarily change statement delimiter\nCREATE PROCEDURE Defines a new stored procedure\nCALL procedure_name(...) Executes a stored procedure\nDROP PROCEDURE Removes an existing procedure• \n• \nSHOW PROCEDURE STATUS WHERE Db ='startersql' ;\nDROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS AddUser ;", "Creating a Procedure with Input Parameters\nLet’s say you want to create a stored procedure that inserts a new user into the \nusers table.\nExample:\nThis creates a procedure named AddUser  that accepts five input parameters.\nCalling the Procedure\nYou can call the procedure using:\nThis will insert the new user into the users table.DELIMITER $$\nCREATE PROCEDURE AddUser (\n    IN p_name VARCHAR (100),\n    IN p_email VARCHAR (100),\n    IN p_gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other'),\n    IN p_dob DATE ,\n    IN p_salary INT\n)\nBEGIN\n    INSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth , salary)\n    VALUES (p_name, p_email , p_gender , p_dob, p_salary );\nEND$$\nDELIMITER ;\nCALL AddUser ('Kiran Sharma' ,'kiran@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1994-06-15' ,72000);", 'Triggers in MySQL\nA trigger  is a special kind of stored program that is automatically executed\n(triggered)  when a specific event occurs in a table — such as INSERT, UPDATE, or \nDELETE.\nTriggers are commonly used for:\nLogging changes\nEnforcing additional business rules\nAutomatically updating related data\nBasic Trigger Structure\nTriggers can be fired:\nBEFORE or AFTER an event\nOn INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE\nScenario: Log Every New User Insertion\nSuppose we want to log every time a new user is inserted into the users table.\nWe’ll create a separate table called user_log  to store log entries.• \n• \n• \nCREATE TRIGGER trigger_name\nAFTER INSERT ON table_name\nFOR EACH ROW\nBEGIN\n-- statements to execute\nEND;\n• \n• ']                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Changing the delimiter is necessary because MySQL normally uses the semicolon (`;`) to mark the end of a statement. When you define a stored procedure, the procedure body itself contains many `;` characters to terminate the individual SQL statements inside the `BEGIN … END` block. If the default delimiter were left unchanged, MySQL would interpret the first `;` it encounters inside the procedure as the end of the whole `CREATE PROCEDURE` statement, causing a syntax error. By temporarily setting a different delimiter (e.g., `$$` or `//`) before the `CREATE PROCEDURE` command and restoring `;` afterward, you tell MySQL to treat the entire block—including its internal `;` characters—as a single statement. (Source: MySQL Handbook.pdf, Page 64) | Because statements inside the procedure also end with a semicolon, which would confuse MySQL, so a temporary delimiter like $$ is used. |     nan        |          nan        |
| How do I run a stored procedure?                                                   | ['Stored Procedures in MySQL\nA stored procedure  is a saved SQL block that can be executed later. This\ncan confuse MySQL. To avoid this, we temporarily change the delimiter  (e.g.\xa0to \n$$ or //) while creating the procedure.\nSyntax for Creating a Stored Procedure\nAfter the procedure is created, we reset the delimiter back to ;.DELIMITER $$\nCREATE PROCEDURE procedure_name ()\nBEGIN\n-- SQL statements go here\nEND$$\nDELIMITER ;', "Creating a Procedure with Input Parameters\nLet’s say you want to create a stored procedure that inserts a new user into the \nusers table.\nExample:\nThis creates a procedure named AddUser  that accepts five input parameters.\nCalling the Procedure\nYou can call the procedure using:\nThis will insert the new user into the users table.DELIMITER $$\nCREATE PROCEDURE AddUser (\n    IN p_name VARCHAR (100),\n    IN p_email VARCHAR (100),\n    IN p_gender ENUM ('Male','Female' ,'Other'),\n    IN p_dob DATE ,\n    IN p_salary INT\n)\nBEGIN\n    INSERT INTO users (name, email, gender, date_of_birth , salary)\n    VALUES (p_name, p_email , p_gender , p_dob, p_salary );\nEND$$\nDELIMITER ;\nCALL AddUser ('Kiran Sharma' ,'kiran@example.com' ,'Female' ,'1994-06-15' ,72000);", "Notes\nInput parameters are declared using the IN keyword.\nStored procedures are stored in the database and can be reused.\nViewing Stored Procedures\nDropping a Stored Procedure\nSummary\nCommand Purpose\nDELIMITER $$ Temporarily change statement delimiter\nCREATE PROCEDURE Defines a new stored procedure\nCALL procedure_name(...) Executes a stored procedure\nDROP PROCEDURE Removes an existing procedure• \n• \nSHOW PROCEDURE STATUS WHERE Db ='startersql' ;\nDROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS AddUser ;", 'Triggers in MySQL\nA trigger  is a special kind of stored program that is automatically executed\n(triggered)  when a specific event occurs in a table — such as INSERT, UPDATE, or \nDELETE.\nTriggers are commonly used for:\nLogging changes\nEnforcing additional business rules\nAutomatically updating related data\nBasic Trigger Structure\nTriggers can be fired:\nBEFORE or AFTER an event\nOn INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE\nScenario:
